newsitem.title: UK: Subdued UK PPIs strengthen case for steady rates.
newsitem.headline: Subdued UK PPIs strengthen case for steady rates.

text.p: British producer price data for December show inflationary pressures remain subdued and will strengthen Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke's hand in resisting pressure to raise interest rates this week.
"Given the strength of oil prices over December, the 0.5 percent fall in input prices was pretty impressive," said Philip Shaw, chief economist at Union Plc.
"This will buy some time for the chancellor so that he will be able to wait for the Q4 GDP figures before deciding whether a tightening in monetary policy is needed."
David Coleman of CIBC Wood Gundy noted that the underlying input price index, excluding food, drink, tobacco and petroleum, was down 0.9 percent month-on-moonth.
"Taken together, the figures suggest that manufacturers are enjoying low raw material costs despite the pickup in energy prices and keeping their output prices under tight rein," he said.

"A more revealing test will come with the January data and the annual revision of manufacturers' price lists. But today's figures will provide the Chancellor with another excuse to keep interest rates on hold, should he so wish."
Clarke meets Bank of England Governor Eddie George at around 1500 GMT on Wednesday for their monthly monetary meeting.

The central bank has made clear it believes interest rates should rise further from the present 6.0 percent level to prevent a resurgence of inflation, which is above the government target at the retail price level.

Some economists believe Clarke will delay any move until February, by which time he will have seen preliminary fourth-quarter GDP data due on January 27. Output prices were up 0.5 percent in December on an unadjusted basis.
Seasonally adjusted output prices excluding food, drink, tobacco and petroleum were up 0.1 percent.
"The quarter-on-quarter annualised rate of growth was only 1.1 percent," said Andrew Milligan of General Accident.
"The outlook is good as the latest upturn in the CBI survey of price expectations is quite normal as list prices are increased at the turn of the year."

Shaw noted that PPI pressures had been subdued for over a year now but this had failed to show up in retail prices. RPIX, the government target measure which excludes mortgage interest payments, was 3.3 percent year-on-year in November.
"One would imagine that the PPIs will have an impact on inflation at the high street level over the coming months and put downward pressure on RPIX," Shaw said.

"Having said that, it's still extremely unlikely that we'll see the government's target being met by the end of this parliament." The RPIX target is 2.5 percent or less. Jonathan Loynes of HSBC Markets expects the sharp drop in factory gate inflation to feed into retail prices in 1997, allowing the RPIX to fall even as activity gathers pace.
He noted that all of the upward pressure on the input side came from fuel.
"The non-oil commodity environment remains extremely benign," Loynes said, adding that the strength of sterling was keeping costs in industry under heavy downward pressure.
"Overall, these data provide further confirmation that pipeline inflation presuress remain extremely weak," he said.
"Coupled with last week's softer than expected data on manufacturing output and Christmas retail sales, the figures ease the pressure for a rise in interest rates after Wednesday's monetary meeting."
